paragraphs: Once they entered Hebei, graves began to multiply beside the road.

Some were no more than three stones piled together; others bore scraps of wooden markers. Fu Rong looked at them so long from the saddle that at last a clerk riding beside him explained. These were the unclaimed graves left from the years when the armies of Yan had scattered. The dead had been buried wherever they fell. Later, when Qin repaired the official roads, some were moved, and moved again, until the living no longer knew where their dead lay.
“Does the administration in Ye have records of them?” Fu Rong asked.
The clerk shook his head. On one low mound lay two fresh cakes, their edges already pecked by birds. Fu Rong asked nothing more and urged his horse east.

He had left Chang’an under imperial orders with only twenty feathered-guard cavalrymen, officers of the Court of Judicial Review, and two clerks practiced in auditing military registers. Changing horses along the way, they reached Ye in eight days. As the walls emerged in the distance, reeds on the northern bank of the Zhang River were deep green, and the wind turned the leaves of the grain silver across the shallows. Yet there was no music inside the city. Market gates were shut and half the horse market stood empty. Two wooden barriers divided the entrance: registered Di military households were sent one way, Xianbei households another. The Xianbei were searched especially closely; even women’s garments were pulled apart and inspected.
A new board stood beside the gate: “If men of Yan conceal armor, punishment shall extend to three branches of their kin.”

Beneath it knelt three bound prisoners. Blood darkened the old man’s back; the two younger men beside him had cracked lips. The commandant at the gate explained that arrowheads had been found in their cart. They were suspected of involvement in the arsenal fire.

Fu Rong picked up an arrowhead between his fingers. Rust had eaten into the iron, the edge was blunt, and old soil clung to the socket. It had plainly lain buried for years. He asked the old man where he had found it.

“In a grave,” the man answered. “My son died the year Yan fell. We could not even recover all his bones. I buried a few arrows beside the mound so I could find it on his death day. This year the officials ordered us to move the graves. I dug them up and took them with me.”
The commandant barked at the prisoner to stop his lies. Fu Rong turned to him. “Did the county order you to search for weapons, or to dig through other men’s graves?”
The commandant had no answer.
“Untie them. Bring a physician. Take down that board.”
“My lord, these are urgent orders from the governor’s office.”
“If the governor objects, he may come and speak to me.”

The old man, freed of his bonds, stooped to gather his arrows. The younger men supported him toward the crowd. As they reached the barriers, a soldier instinctively thrust out an arm to block the Xianbei passage. Fu Rong did not rebuke him. He simply ordered the commandant to pull down both fences.

The city gate suddenly stood wide, but no one moved. First a cart driver from the Di queue hesitantly drove through. Then a Xianbei woman, leading a child, passed slowly beneath an arch she had not been allowed to use before. The soldiers watched them sidelong but did not interfere. The child looked back at Fu Rong as if he were no prince at all, only a stranger who had moved a wooden fence.

Du Mian, governor of Wei Commandery, waited outside his office. At Fu Rong’s first question about the arsenal, his prepared words of welcome became useless. He hurried to take the visitor’s reins and lead the way. Near the abandoned palace of Yan in the north of the city, part of the western storehouse roof had collapsed and its walls were blackened; the eastern storehouse was untouched. Guards stood rigidly alert in the courtyard, while the houses beyond had been sealed off in several rings.

Fu Rong stepped across the burned threshold and crouched to take a handful of ash. It was light and powdery; none of the grease from burned leather armor stained his fingers, nor did he find charcoal left by bowstrings or arrow shafts. Pale rectangular marks ran along the base of the wall, clean inside, gray with ash outside. Wooden chests had once stood there and had clearly been moved before the fire.
“How many weapons were kept here?”

The storehouse registrar turned the pages and answered quickly: more than a thousand spears, over a hundred crossbows, and upward of a hundred thousand arrows, most in the eastern storehouse. The official accounts were intact. The fire had struck the western building, where no substantial stock of weapons appeared in the inventory.
“If the inventory contains no such weapons, how does the court know any have disappeared?” Fu Rong asked.
Sweat broke out on the registrar’s forehead. “Commandant Feng reported them before he died. He said a consignment of armor and arms was being held temporarily.”
“Held for whom?”
“He said it was by order from above.”
“Which order from above?”

The registrar dropped to his knees and dared say no more. Feng Du, the commandant responsible for the warehouse, was dead, his body found at the bottom of a dry well west of the city. Fu Rong ordered an inventory of the registered weapons and forbade anyone to move the remaining chests. He then walked around the rear of the building. The inside of the door bolt had splintered; grooves in the wood showed where heavy boxes had been dragged. Oil had been poured in the northwest corner, and the flames had consumed records and old wagon gear while leaving the beams blackened but not burned through. Beneath the eaves along the courtyard wall, narrow wheel ruts survived until the rain-washed entrance. A fleck of dark red paint remained on the stone sill.
“That is not the black paint used on warehouse carts,” the registrar said quietly.

Fu Rong wrapped the fleck and had an officer preserve it. He named no suspect. Instead he asked Du Mian, “If you knew weapons were being taken out of the warehouse, why were you examining which Xianbei came in and out of the city?”
Du Mian’s face tightened. Rumor said the soldiers of Yan were preparing to rebel, he replied. Without immediate arrests, there might be an uprising before dawn.
“What have your searches uncovered?”
“Bows, swords ... and some old military banners.”
“Were all of them brought here recently?”
“Not all.”
“Did you send anyone after the carts carrying the armor?”
“As soon as I sealed the city, I sent—”
“Whose city did you seal?”

Du Mian could no longer meet his gaze. Outside, the people from neighboring houses were peering past the official seals. Fu Rong remembered his brother’s instruction before he left Chang’an: do not begin by arresting people. Only now did he understand how hard it was to follow. Those truly frightened in Ye were not confined to one side of the wooden barriers. If weapons appeared in the streets that night, the swords already at the ready on both sides would have no interest in where they had come from.

The governor’s office had kept seventeen copied pages from an old register. The original had perished on the night of the fire. So many hands had turned the copies that their corners looked nibbled by mice. Fu Rong opened the first. It recorded a former Left Guard military household of Yan, surnamed Wang: originally from Liaoxi, now living in Ye, mother alive, elder brother lost in Hedong. On the next page was a former cavalryman with a lame leg, a daughter married in Zhongshan, and a younger brother dead in a place unknown. The pages were crowded with relatives' names, their present homes, and the years in which they had gone missing. Small notes had been added: “two measures of grain,” “one bolt of cloth,” “found.”

On the seventh page, the ink changed abruptly. In the margin someone had added, “Able to ride; bow.” The eighth said, “Strong; fit to fight.” On the final page appeared instructions about a white feather as a signal and three drumbeats at the east gate. The sharp strokes seemed hacked into the page in haste.

The copyist knelt below the steps. Fu Rong called him nearer. The man was ordinarily invisible in the governor’s offices, but when the matter turned to handwriting, a stubbornness emerged. Taking out his worn brush, he dipped it in ink and demonstrated on a scrap of paper.

“The names were mostly written with an old brush. The ink was mixed with glue, which turns gray over time. Whoever added the secret messages used new, stiff bristles. The point was sharp and the finishing strokes too hurried. The words were squeezed into spaces already there; even the character for 'gate' has been written crooked. I reported this discrepancy before.”
Du Mian frowned. “You said the handwriting differed. You never said the record was forged.”
“I did not dare say it was forged,” the copyist replied, lowering his head. “I said only that it did not look like the work of one hand.”

Fu Rong held the two sheets together in the daylight. The ink was indeed different. Yet different handwriting did not prove a forgery; many people might have worked on the old register, and someone might later have used it to contact former soldiers. Rather than decide at once, he ordered three households named in the pages brought before him.

A Xianbei widow came first. She was hard of hearing and made the clerk repeat his questions several times. Fu Rong pointed to two ink circles beside her name. Those, she explained, marked relief grain received. Her husband had died and the family had no land. Men of Yan at the horse market had pooled grain for them, marking a circle for each distribution. Beside a one-eyed veteran’s name stood two horizontal strokes: the first recorded news of his nephew, the second confirmed the nephew’s death. A young man in his twenties, asked why his name bore the words “Strong; fit to fight,” looked bewildered. He and his mother had come the previous year seeking his uncle’s grave. They would have had to make the journey in the fiercest summer heat, and it was only through this register that they had found the right place.
“Where was your uncle buried?” Fu Rong asked.
“In Hedong. Among the nameless graves beside the official road.”
“Have you been there?”

The young man nodded and took a small wooden plaque from his robe. His uncle’s name was cut into it in crooked strokes made with his own knife. His mother had gone there to make offerings last year. She was certain, at last, that her brother had come home.
As the widow was leaving the hall, she turned back and asked the clerk, “Sir, my other son has still not been found. If the register is destroyed, who will help me look for him?”

The clerk glanced instinctively at Fu Rong. Fu Rong instructed them to copy the missing son’s name, former residence, and year of displacement onto a sheet the widow could keep herself. Whatever the outcome of the inquiry, the two clerks from the Department of State Affairs were to make separate copies of the entries in the seventeen pages concerning lost relatives and relief grain.
The widow folded her sheet until it was very small and tucked it against her chest. She could scarcely read, but she pressed the paper there with both hands.
Only then did Fu Rong order Muyu An brought in. Du Mian looked troubled: the prisoner was severely injured and could not travel, he said; it would be better to question him in prison.

The prison in Ye leaned against the old palace wall. Years of cold damp had covered its stonework with green moss. Muyu An was chained in its deepest cell, both knees swollen out of shape and black scabs crusted across his wounded fingers. When he heard the door, he did not struggle. He merely opened his eyes and looked at those who had come.
“Prince of Yangping?”
“Yes.”
“So Chang’an has finally decided to ask me something?”

Fu Rong studied his injuries and first demanded to know who had ordered the torture. The jailer and Du Mian tried to shift blame between them. Fu Rong made an officer of the Court of Judicial Review record their statements on the spot and ordered the interrogator held for questioning. Only then did he sit beside the prisoner’s couch.

Muyu An explained that when Yan fell, the families of former soldiers had been scattered in every direction. He and Yue Shou had collected grain and searched for the missing, first noting their old units and homes in a single book, then making three copies for Ye, Zhongshan, and Hedong. Some men had hidden swords in the rafters and buried arrows in their courtyards. Some dreamed of restoring Yan; others feared only that soldiers would come for them in the night. He would not swear that every man of Yan was free of rebellious thoughts, but he was certain the phrases about the white feather had never been in the original register.
“How did the original come into another man’s possession?” Fu Rong asked.

“The day before the fire, a merchant came with a letter from Yue Shou asking to borrow it. He said the court was checking military households again, and unless our records were compared with the official ones, we might be listed as fugitives.”
“Did you know the merchant?”
“No. He had a Guanzhong accent. Part of his left ear was missing.”
“And the letter?”
“The governor’s officers took it.”
Du Mian protested at once that he had never seen such a letter. Muyu An closed his eyes and gave a faint laugh; the movement tugged at his wounds, and blood appeared at his lips.

Fu Rong held water to his mouth. Muyu An could swallow only a little, and it took him a long while to recover. Fu Rong asked whether anyone had urged him to raise troops. No, he said. Then he lifted his mangled hand and pointed toward the copied pages on the table.
“If I truly meant to rebel, why would I write down where our wives and children lived, ready for your men to seize them?”
“If you meant to save people, why record the old military units?”
“Among men lost from the army, only comrades of the same old unit know where to look. That is how we recognize one another.”
Fu Rong heard the wounded pride in his voice. He did not say whether the method was dangerous. He asked instead, “Then why did you hand the real register to a stranger?”
Tears filled Muyu An’s eyes. A commandant who had survived decades of war seemed more ashamed at this question than at anything his torturers had done to him.

“I was afraid,” he said. “Wang Jinglüe was dying. Everyone in the city said the government in Chang’an was about to change. That man had Yue Shou’s letter, and he said he could keep us alive. I believed him.”

Fu Rong meant to ask more about the carts of armor, but Muyu An’s breath had become shallow. Catching the prince’s sleeve, he spoke one word at a time. “There are men waiting for us to draw our swords first. The more you arrest, the more our children are afraid to go outside. The more they hide, the more certain you become that something is happening ... When that day comes, who will remember which night the first fire was lit?”
He had scarcely finished when a fit of coughing brought blood from his mouth and his fingers fell open. The physician had not yet reached the deepest cell when Muyu An died.

Fu Rong sat beside him for a long time, then picked up a copied page spattered with blood. At the top was the name of a military settler whose entry had once read, “Burial place unknown.” The spreading blood had now made even his name hard to read.
He put the sheet inside the case file. As he left the prison he said only, “Record precisely how Muyu An died. You will not write 'died of illness.'”

That afternoon, Fu Rong examined the body of Feng Du, the warehouse commandant. Feng had been found in a well behind an abandoned dye works. There was a ligature mark around his neck, but the soles of his shoes were clean: his body had been disposed of after death. His commandant’s tally was missing. Red paint resembling that on the stone sill of the warehouse marked both the well rim and the broken gateway of the dye works. Beyond it, hastily swept wheel tracks led toward an old landing on the Zhang River.

They followed the traces to the riverbank. The mooring posts bore fresh rope marks, but the mud held none of the deep furrows that heavy cargo would have left while being loaded. Fu Rong crouched beside the water and watched a boatman pole an empty skiff through floating duckweed. If dozens of carts laden with armor had been loaded here, the shallow Zhang would have borne the marks of dragging them down to the boats. Apart from scattered wheel and hoof prints, there was nothing.
“Someone wanted us to look toward the river,” an officer said quietly.

Fu Rong nodded, but would not declare a destination on that evidence alone. He questioned the families living near the bank. Several said they had seen no carts or horses on the night of the fire. As he questioned more of them, their answers began to sound rehearsed. At dusk a boy who had been gathering firewood and tending sheep was brought before him, clutching half a cold cake to his chest.

The boy said that on the night of the fire he had been searching the embankment for a lost sheep. He had seen seven carts turn away from the old landing toward the south. They were covered with hemp cloth and drawn by oxen straining at their yokes. Someone had shouted at him to leave and threatened to have his father imprisoned if he told the authorities.
“Seven carts?” Fu Rong asked.

The boy held out his grimy fingers and counted them one by one. When he came to the last cart, he drew a circle in the air. “That one had red around its wheels. Like the coaches the great officials bring from Chang’an—red so dark it was nearly black.”
“Aren’t you afraid I might arrest your father too?”
The boy shivered. Fu Rong handed him a hot cake. “If you are afraid, you need say no more. I will record what you have already told me.”
But the boy pointed south. “They stopped at the old brick kilns. The third opening.”

The kilns had lain abandoned for years. After dark the grass reached the bellies of the horses. By torchlight the party entered the third kiln and met a rank smell. Two bodies lay beneath rotten straw, their throats cut; one wore a cart driver’s clothes, the other a coarse short jacket. Broken boards were scattered across the floor, some still bearing clay seals from the arsenal, though the impressions had been scraped away. The killers had taken the weapons, but not every trace of their passage.

Searching the dead men’s clothing, an officer found a bronze tag on the driver. Its face had been filed smooth, but the reverse still bore the inscription “Imperial Clan Office, C-21.” Dark red paint clung to the edge, nearly the same shade as the fleck from the warehouse sill.
The torch in Du Mian’s hand wavered.
“A tally of the Fu imperial clan,” he said.
“Or someone wishes us to believe it is,” Fu Rong replied.
“It was cast by the Imperial Clan Office. How could an ordinary man obtain one?”
“More men can lay hands on a tally than those who live in a prince’s house. A driver, a storekeeper, a man who borrows a cart, a man who steals one—which of them could not find a way?”

Fu Rong put the tag into a small box and ordered the kiln sealed and evidence recorded. No rumor was to be spread. Back in the city, he first ordered the temporary checkpoints that divided travelers by ancestry removed, and reviewed the cases of everyone arrested solely because a name appeared in the register. Anyone actually found hiding new armor, killing or setting fires would still be prosecuted on evidence. Officials complained that releasing prisoners now would anger Di military households. Fu Rong kept the night patrols in place, but had the wooden posts dividing the peoples pulled up. The city did not grow peaceful overnight. In several lanes people still guarded their doors with clubs and carried children into the back rooms whenever they heard hooves.

A Xianbei woman came to the government gate to reclaim her detained husband. Seeing two Di soldiers looking her way, she drew back into the shadow of the wall. Neither soldier would approach her; they spoke to one another from across the street. Fu Rong watched from a window. He had removed the wooden barriers, but the barriers in people’s minds rose higher than the city walls.

That night he ordered his clerks to copy the missing persons, widows, orphans, and grain recipients from the mutual-aid register exactly as they had originally been recorded. Where old units were known, the government would keep that information under seal for verification, but it would not be posted publicly. A family looking for its missing kin needed only names, relationships, and last known whereabouts. He also divided the proceedings into two cases: possible unlawful possession of weapons by former Yan military households would be investigated on evidence, while the torture that had caused a prisoner’s death would be examined separately. Du Mian was displeased but dared not object.

He worked on his secret report far into the night. By lamplight Fu Rong listed the registered weapons still intact, the unregistered arms carried away, the fire set to hide their removal, the suspicious additions to the register, and the uncertain origin of the Imperial Clan Office tag. Then he recorded the arrested widow, Muyu An’s death, and the fear that had turned one military household against another. He wrote no culprit’s name. After a pause he added a line: “To declare this a rebellion of the Yan people before the inquiry is complete may be precisely what the plotters intend. Punish no one on grounds of ancestry. Do not summon Murong Chui for questioning without cause.”
The ink had not yet dried when armor clattered outside his door.

A commandant of the feathered guard entered and knelt. A merchant had been detained in the south of the city, a man with part of his left ear missing and a Guanzhong accent. His travel permit came from an old merchant house in Chang’an.
“Where is he?”
“At the post house. When they searched him he crushed something between his teeth.”

Fu Rong took a lamp and hurried there. The man was pinned to a couch, his face turning blue, froth gathering at his throat. A physician forced open his jaw and extracted half a bead of broken wax and a trace of black poison. Bending close, Fu Rong asked who had given him Yue Shou’s letter, where he had taken the borrowed register, and which city gate the carts of armor had passed through. The merchant’s eyes wandered. He seemed to want to speak, but only bloody foam came from his mouth.
Fu Rong asked once more. “Is your master in Chang’an?”

The merchant’s lips moved. The sound was too faint to distinguish: it might have been the word for a noble lord, or the word for the palace. Before a syllable was formed, his neck stiffened, and he died.
The room was so quiet that Fu Rong could hear the physician set down his bowl.

The documents, seals, and money taken from the merchant were all genuine, yet none pointed to a single man. Someone outside the city had borrowed merchant carts, a tally familiar to the gate officers, and trade routes worn smooth by years of use. With these he had obtained a real register, added false secret orders, and left real corpses behind him. Standing before the evidence, Fu Rong found that genuine things altered by a cunning hand were harder to untangle than ordinary forgeries.

He returned to the governor’s office after the third night watch. The soldiers on the wall had just changed guard, and the sound of the east gate locking drifted through the darkness. Several clerks went pale at the mention of those secret instructions about the gate. Fu Rong did not laugh at them. He too looked east until he heard the gate officer call the customary all-clear, and only then entered the hall.

At one end of the desk lay the Imperial Clan Office tally; at the other was the widow’s sheet listing her missing son. Fu Rong added the seven carts, the abandoned kiln, and the merchant’s death by poison to his report, sealed the dispatch box, and sent a trusted rider west toward Chang’an before dawn.

As the rider was leaving, a clerk stopped him. What should be entered for the burial place of the widow’s second son? Fu Rong took the sheet, studied the empty space at the end, and asked, “Have you found anything?”
“No, my lord.”
“Then leave it blank. Write only as far as the inquiry has reached.”
The clerk dipped his brush again and carefully set down the widow’s name. For the son lost so many years ago, he did not invent a resting place.
Dawn was near and the oil in the hall lamps was almost spent. Fu Rong poured in another ladle and ordered the writing to continue.
